title: What Darwin Really Thought About Human Nature
the_thought: He thought people are animals who learned to be kind.
hook: A brown notebook. Two words in pencil. I think. Under them Darwin drew a fork of ink, a tree with no names. He has already sailed around the world. He has watched a boy who was bought for a button put on English clothes and take them off again. He is asking the only human nature question that tree is for. If every living thing sits on one fork, where do we sit? And what does that make us? People later said he taught that we are just selfish animals. He thought people are animals who learned to be kind. That is the thought. The rest is how a shy man spent his life proving the first half, and then the second.

levels.name: I Think
beats: July 1837. Darwin is back in London. The voyage on HMS Beagle is over. He buys little notebooks that fit a pocket. In notebook B, on a page he numbered 36, he writes two words. I think. Under them he draws a branching tree. It is not a ladder. There is no gold star at the top for us. It is a fork. Lineages split. Some die. Some keep going. On another page in the same book he writes that it is absurd to talk of one animal being higher than another. That line is the quiet bomb. If we are not higher by magic, we are on the fork too. He has not published On the Origin of Species. That book is still twenty-two years away. He is already asking what human nature is if we are not a special clay. The notebook sits on a desk. The ink is cheap. The idea is not. Later people will print the page and call it the tree of life. In the room it is just a doodle with two words on top. I think. He is not sure. That is why the words are there. He is a shy man who likes worms and barnacles. He is also a man who has seen enough faces to doubt the old story that we were dropped in last, finished, apart. The fork says we were not dropped. We grew. And if we grew, then pride, fear, love, and shame grew too. That is a human nature claim, even before he dares to print the word man on a title page. Keep the picture. A pale Y of ink. Two words. A man who is not preaching. He is thinking. The rest of his life is him trying to make that doodle safe enough to say in public, and then trying to say what it does to us. He does not yet have a public theory of selection. He has a picture. The picture is enough to ruin the old boast that we stand apart by kind.

levels.name: Jemmy Button
beats: The fork did not start on paper. It started on a wet deck. Captain Robert FitzRoy of HMS Beagle had taken hostages from Tierra del Fuego after a boat was stolen. One of them was a Yahgan boy named Orundellico. The crew called him Jemmy Button because FitzRoy paid for him with a large pearl button. They took him to England, dressed him, taught him English, even showed him at court. When Darwin boarded for the second voyage, Jemmy was on the ship in a coat and boots, speaking English. Darwin wrote that a few years had been enough to change the habits. Then they reached the south. Darwin looked at the people on the shore and used a hard period word, savage, the word his century used when it wanted a gap. He was shocked. He also could not unsee the boy at the table. Same kind of human. Clothes and forks are not a species. Months later the Beagle came back. The little mission had failed. Jemmy had taken off the dress coat. Darwin wrote of a complete and grievous change. He told his sister the clean stout lad was now thin. Then Jemmy sat down, used a knife and fork, and said he was very happy. He did not wish to return to England. He had married. Darwin's diary is not a speech about human nature, and we should not invent one. What we have is the shock, the clothes, the return, and the later books that refuse a wall between kinds of people. In Brazil he had already watched slavery and hated it. The Wedgwood family he came from had made the abolition medallion. A man can hate chains and still rank cultures. Darwin did both. Hold the button. A boy was priced like a trinket. The naturalist still had to decide if that boy sat on a different branch. He decided he did not.

levels.name: Light Thrown
beats: In 1859 he finally prints On the Origin of Species. He almost leaves us out. He writes that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history. That is the whole tease. He had told Charles Lyell he would avoid the whole subject of man, because it was wrapped in prejudice. Punch magazine still drew monkeys in coats. Reviewers asked what a man may become if a monkey became a man. Everyone heard the missing chapter. Alfred Russel Wallace, the other man who found natural selection, later flinched. By the late 1860s Wallace said the human brain was too big for selection alone. He talked about spirit. He wanted a gap after all. Darwin did not take the gap. In 1871 he publishes The Descent of Man. He says he once thought a hint in Origin was enough. Now the case looks different. He writes that man must be included with other living things in any general conclusion. Light was not a polite cough. Light was the fork drawn in 1837, finally said in public. Wallace stays a friend and a problem. Darwin will not put a ghost on the last branch to save our pride. That is the middle of the thought. We are not a side project. We are on the same tree. If you want a magic wall around human nature, you will not get it from him. You will get a book that takes twelve years after Origin to dare the word man in the title, and then does not blink.

levels.name: Moral Sense
beats: Here is the line people skip when they want a mean Darwin. He says the difference in mind between us and the higher animals, great as it is, is one of degree and not of kind. Love, memory, curiosity, even a kind of reason, he says, show up in animals, sometimes only a little, sometimes a lot. Then he names the biggest difference. The moral sense. Conscience. The short word ought. He does not say it fell from the sky. He says any animal with strong social instincts, once its mind got sharp, would grow a conscience. First you like your pack. You help them. You feel with them. Then you remember. Then you talk. Then habit makes the feeling stick. He says those instincts, plus a working mind, plus habit, lead to the golden rule. Do to others what you would have them do to you. That, he writes, sits at the foundation of morality. Kindness is not a miracle bolted onto a beast. Kindness is the pack learning to keep the feeling when the hunger has passed. In 1872 he publishes The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals. He watches his own babies. He watches dogs. A face that bares teeth in a grin is not only ours. A dog that looks ashamed is not a cartoon we invented. He is not saying a dog writes laws. He is saying the raw stuff of human nature is older than the courtroom. The fork did not stop at bones. It ran through the face, and then through the feeling that says you should not hurt the one who eats beside you.

levels.name: False Fitness
beats: Then the story gets stolen. Herbert Spencer had already coined survival of the fittest. Darwin later uses the phrase for nature. Other men turn it into a slogan for leaving the poor to die. They call that Social Darwinism. It is not the book he wrote about conscience. He did not say a factory owner is a lion. He said sympathy started with the same group, and that reason could push it out to a whole nation, and then, if we let it, to people of every nation and race. He even said kindness to animals was a late moral gain. That is the pack getting bigger, not a license to kick. And still there is a stain. Darwin used the ranking words of his century. Civilized. Savage. Grades of nations. Later racists quoted those pages and skipped the golden rule. He also argued we are one species, and that the old fight over many Adams would die when evolution was accepted. Both things are in the same man. We should not wash the stain. We should not let the slogan eat the thought. He thought people are animals who learned to be kind. The fork includes us. The button was never a different branch. The notebook still sits in Cambridge. Anyone can look at the two words. I think. Under them the pale fork. That is human nature as he drew it. Not an angel. Not a wolf with a speech. An animal that can remember the pack when the pack gets bigger. That is what he thought about human nature. Not a sermon. A fork, a button, a book he was afraid to write, and then a book he did.
What he thought about God is another story. That one is next.
